hints: Picture each halogen at room temperature and link colour to state, chlorine is a gas, bromine is a liquid, iodine is a solid.
walkthrough:
Recall what you see in the lab**
Think of the three halogens side by side. Chlorine is a pale yellow-green gas, bromine is a fuming orange to brown liquid, and iodine is a shiny grey-black solid that gives a purple vapour.
Final answer: Chlorine is yellow-green, bromine is orange/brown/red, iodine is grey/black (silver-grey solid).

hints: Remember an oxidising agent gains electrons, so think about how easily each halogen atom attracts an electron down the group.
walkthrough:
Link oxidising power to electron gain**
An oxidising agent oxidises another species by taking electrons from it, so the halogen itself is reduced to $X^-$. The better it is at attracting an electron, the stronger the oxidiser.

Apply the Group 17 trend**
Down the group atomic size increases and the incoming electron is further from the nucleus with more shielding, so electron affinity becomes less favourable. Chlorine is therefore the strongest oxidiser and iodine the weakest.
Final answer: Oxidising strength decreases from chlorine to iodine.

hints: Start from the colour of chlorine gas and think about the colour of the hydrogen chloride product formed.
walkthrough:
Visualise the reaction**
Chlorine is a yellow-green gas, $\text{Cl}_2(g)$, while hydrogen is colourless and the product hydrogen chloride, $\text{HCl}(g)$, is also colourless. When $\text{H}_2 + \text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{HCl}$, the only coloured species is used up, so the green colour fades away.
Final answer: The green colour disappears / decolourises.

hints: Focus on the bond that must break when HX decomposes and how halogen atomic size changes down the group.
walkthrough:
Identify the key bond**
Thermal decomposition of a hydrogen halide breaks the $\text{H-X}$ bond, for example $2\text{HI} \rightarrow \text{H}_2 + \text{I}_2$. Stability therefore depends directly on how strong that $\text{H-X}$ bond is.

Explain why bond strength falls**
Down the group the halogen atom gets larger, so the overlap between the hydrogen $1s$ orbital and the halogen $p$ orbital becomes poorer and the bond gets longer and weaker. $\text{H-Cl}$ is strongest, $\text{H-I}$ is weakest, so stability decreases from $\text{HCl}$ to $\text{HI}$.
Final answer: The $\text{H-X}$ covalent bond strength decreases down the group, so less energy is needed to break it.

hints: Think about what homolytic fission produces and what is unusual about the electron arrangement in that species.
walkthrough:
Define in one precise phrase**
A free radical such as $\text{Cl}^\bullet$ is formed when a covalent bond splits evenly. Each atom keeps one electron from the pair, leaving a highly reactive species with a single unpaired electron, shown by the dot.
Final answer: A species with one or more unpaired electrons.

hints: Think about what type of energy is needed at room temperature to split $\text{Cl}_2$ into $\text{Cl}^\bullet$ radicals by homolysis.
walkthrough:
Connect energy to bond breaking**
Alkanes do not react with chlorine in the dark at room temperature because the $\text{Cl-Cl}$ bond needs energy to break homolytically: $\text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{Cl}^\bullet$. Ultraviolet light provides exactly the energy needed for this initiation step.
Final answer: Ultraviolet light / UV / sunlight.

hints: Recall that each propagation step uses one radical and makes a new radical, keeping the chain going.
First a $\text{Cl}^\bullet$ abstracts H from $\text{C}_2\text{H}_6$, then the resulting carbon radical reacts with $\text{Cl}_2$ to give the product and regenerate $\text{Cl}^\bullet$.
walkthrough:
Write the first propagation, hydrogen abstraction**
The chlorine radical attacks ethane and removes a hydrogen atom. The $\text{C-H}$ bond breaks and a new $\text{H-Cl}$ bond forms, leaving an ethyl radical: $$\text{C}_2\text{H}_6 + \text{Cl}^\bullet \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_5^\bullet + \text{HCl}$$

Write the second propagation, chlorine transfer**
The ethyl radical now attacks a chlorine molecule. It takes one Cl to form chloroethane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$, and kicks out a fresh $\text{Cl}^\bullet$ to continue the chain: $$\text{C}_2\text{H}_5^\bullet + \text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Cl} + \text{Cl}^\bullet$$

Final answer: $\mathrm{C_2H_6 + Cl^\bullet \rightarrow C_2H_5^\bullet + HCl}$
$\mathrm{C_2H_5^\bullet + Cl_2 \rightarrow C_2H_5Cl + Cl^\bullet}$

hints: Think about the reaction of chlorine with aqueous sodium hydroxide and how temperature controls whether chlorate(I) or chlorate(V) forms.
walkthrough:
Choose the correct alkali condition**
Chlorine disproportionates in aqueous sodium hydroxide. Cold, dilute $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ gives sodium chlorate(I), $\text{NaClO}$, plus $\text{NaCl}$ and water: $\text{Cl}_2 + 2\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{NaCl} + \text{NaClO} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$. Hot concentrated alkali would give $\text{NaClO}_3$ instead, so cold conditions are essential.
Final answer: Cold $\text{NaOH(aq)}$.

hints: Think in terms of oxidation numbers and what happens when the same element both increases and decreases in oxidation state.
walkthrough:
State the double change clearly**
Disproportionation means one element starts at one oxidation state and ends up in two different states. In $\text{Cl}_2$ ($0$) $\rightarrow$ $\text{Cl}^-$ ($-1$) + $\text{ClO}^-$ ($+1$), chlorine is both reduced and oxidised at the same time.
Final answer: A reaction in which the same species is both oxidised and reduced simultaneously.

hints: Count chlorine atoms needed to make $\text{CHCl}_3$ and balance sodium and hydroxide around them.
walkthrough:
Balance by atom count**
You need three Cl atoms to make $\text{CHCl}_3$, so you need $3\text{NaClO}$. That gives $3$ Na in total, one ends up in $\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}$ and two in $2\text{NaOH}$, which also balances O and H: $$\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3 + 3\text{NaClO} \rightarrow \text{CHCl}_3 + \text{CH}_3\text{COONa} + 2\text{NaOH}$$
Final answer: $\mathrm{CH_3COCH_3 + 3NaClO \rightarrow CHCl_3 + CH_3COONa + 2NaOH}$

hints: Recall the colour of the silver halide precipitate that indicates chloride ions.
Think about where free $\text{Cl}^-$ ions could come from in aqueous $\text{CHCl}_3$, and what they do with $\text{Ag}^+$.
walkthrough:
State the observation**
A white precipitate appears. In the silver nitrate test, only chloride gives white, bromide gives cream and iodide gives yellow, so this points to $\text{Cl}^-$.

Explain the source of chloride**
$\text{CHCl}_3$ itself contains covalent $\text{C-Cl}$ bonds, not free ions. In aqueous solution it slowly hydrolyses, releasing $\text{Cl}^-(aq)$. These ions then combine with $\text{Ag}^+(aq)$ from $\text{AgNO}_3$: $$\text{Ag}^+(aq) + \text{Cl}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{AgCl}(s)$$ which is seen as the white solid.

Final answer: White precipitate forms.
$\text{CHCl}_3$ is hydrolysed releasing $\text{Cl}^-$ ions which react with $\text{Ag}^+$ to form $\text{AgCl}$.
